claim: P-bodies contain mostly AU-rich mRNAs in human HEK293 cells.
source: We have previously shown that PBs store one third of the coding transcriptome in human epithelial HEK293 cells (Hubstenberger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the P-body transcriptome analysis in HEK293 cells, showing correlation between AU-rich content and PB enrichment (Figure 1B,C).

claim: mRNA accumulation in PBs correlates strongly with their GC content (Spearman r = -0.64, p<0.0001).
source: Most remarkably, mRNA accumulation in PBs was dependent on their global nucleotide composition, with a strong correlation between GC content and PB localization (rs = −0.64, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of transcriptome data showing relationship between GC content and PB enrichment.

claim: Longer mRNAs are more enriched in PBs than shorter ones, with moderate correlation (Spearman r = 0.39, p<0.0001).
source: When mRNAs were subdivided into six classes ranging from <1.5 kb to >10 kb, longer mRNAs appeared more enriched in PBs than shorter ones, with a moderate correlation between length and PB enrichment (Spearman r (rs) = 0.39, p<0.0001) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mRNA length distribution in PB-enriched versus PB-excluded transcripts.

claim: PB mRNAs are longer than PB-excluded mRNAs but shorter than stress granule mRNAs.
source: However, their increased length in PBs was less striking than previously observed for stress granule mRNAs (Khong et al., 2017) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Comparative analysis with published stress granule data from Khong et al., 2017.

claim: mRNA localization in PBs depends on the GC content of both their CDS and 3'UTR.
source: Interestingly, mRNA accumulation in PBs correlated strongly with the GC content of both their CDS and 3'UTR (rs = −0.57 and −0.55, respectively, p<0.0001 for both), and weakly with the one of their 5'UTR (rs = −0.22, p<0.0001) (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of different mRNA regions with PB enrichment.

claim: The lower GC content of PB-enriched mRNAs is independent of their length.
source: Moreover, the lower GC content of PB-enriched mRNAs compared to PB-excluded ones was a feature independent of their length, since it was observed in all length ranges (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Analysis showing GC content differences persist across all mRNA length categories.

claim: PB-enriched mRNAs encode proteins with different amino acid usage compared to PB-excluded mRNAs.
source: Consistently, we found that the frequency of amino acids encoded by GC-rich codons (Ala, Gly, Pro) was lower in PB-stored than in PB-excluded mRNAs, while the frequency of those encoded by AU-rich codons (Lys, Asn) was higher (Figure 2A).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of amino acid frequencies in proteins encoded by PB-enriched versus PB-excluded mRNAs.

claim: Codon usage in PBs is systematically biased towards AU-rich codons.
source: For all amino acids encoded by synonymous codons, the relative codon usage in PBs versus out of PBs was systematically biased towards AU-rich codons (log2 of the ratio >0, Figure 2B).
evidence: Comprehensive analysis of codon usage patterns showing systematic bias toward AU-rich codons in PB mRNAs.

claim: The frequency of low usage codons correlates strongly and negatively with GC3 content.
source: As expected, the frequency of low usage codons correlated strongly and negatively with GC3, with AU-rich CDS having a higher frequency of low usage codons than GC-rich CDS (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between low usage codon frequency and GC content at third codon position.

claim: Protein yield is 20-times lower for PB-enriched than PB-excluded mRNAs.
source: We previously reported that protein yield, defined as the ratio between protein and mRNA abundance in HEK293 cells, was 20-times lower for PB-enriched than PB-excluded mRNAs.
evidence: Reference to previously published data from Hubstenberger et al., 2017.

claim: The low protein yield of PB mRNAs is not due to translational repression within PBs.
source: This was not due to translational repression within PBs, as the proportion of a given mRNA in PBs hardly exceeded 15%, but rather to some intrinsic mRNA property (Hubstenberger et al., 2017).
evidence: Inference based on the observation that only a small fraction of mRNAs are in PBs at any time, combined with citation to previous work.

claim: The number of low usage codons per CDS correlates with both protein yield (rs = -0.46) and PB localization (rs = 0.49).
source: Finally, combining the frequency of low usage codons with the CDS length, that is, considering the absolute number of low usage codons per CDS, was a shared parameter of both protein yield (rs = −0.46, p<0.0001, Figure 2F) and PB localization (rs = 0.49, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis showing relationship between absolute number of low usage codons and both protein yield and PB enrichment.

claim: CDS with more than 100 low usage codons are particularly enriched in PBs.
source: Strikingly, CDS with more than 100 low usage codons were particularly enriched in PBs, while those under 100 were mostly excluded (Figure 2F).
evidence: Quantitative threshold analysis showing distinct PB enrichment patterns based on low usage codon count.

claim: DDX6 expression decreased by 90% in HEK293 cells after siRNA transfection for 48 hours.
source: In these conditions, DDX6 expression decreased by 90% compared to control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot quantification showing DDX6 protein levels after siRNA treatment.

claim: DDX6 depletion did not grossly disturb global translation in HEK293 cells.
source: The polysome profile was largely unaffected by DDX6 silencing, implying that DDX6 depletion did not grossly disturb global translation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Polysome profiling data showing similar profiles in control and DDX6-depleted cells.

claim: DDX6 silencing shows a positive correlation with mRNA GC content for changes in total RNA (rs = 0.45, p<0.0001).
source: Analysis of the whole transcriptome showed a link between mRNA fate following DDX6 depletion and their GC content, but, intriguingly, the correlation was positive for changes in total RNA (rs = 0.45, p<0.0001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of RNA-seq data from DDX6 silencing experiment.

claim: DDX6 silencing shows a negative correlation with mRNA GC content for changes in polysomal RNA (rs = -0.32, p<0.0001).
source: and negative for changes in polysomal RNA (rs = −0.32, p<0.0001; Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of polysomal RNA-seq data from DDX6 silencing experiment.

claim: mRNA stabilization after DDX6 silencing preferentially concerns transcripts with high GC content (>50% GC).
source: The extent of mRNA stabilization steadily increased with the GC content and became predominant for transcripts with >50% GC (Figure 3A, left panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Analysis of fold-changes in mRNA levels after DDX6 silencing stratified by GC content.

claim: DDX6 silencing in K562 cells also shows preferential stabilization of high GC content mRNAs (rs = 0.59, p<0.0001).
source: Despite the differences in cell type, depletion procedure and sequencing methods, again, mRNA stabilization preferentially concerned those with high GC content (rs = 0.59, p<0.0001; Figure 3A, right panel, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A; Supplementary file 1, sheet2).
evidence: Analysis of ENCODE dataset from K562 cells showing similar GC-dependent pattern.

claim: Translation rate predominantly increases for transcripts with less than 45% GC after DDX6 silencing (rs = -0.53, p<0.0001).
source: In contrast, following DDX6 silencing in HEK293 cells, the translation rate predominantly increased for transcripts with less than 45% GC (rs = −0.53, p<0.0001; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Analysis of polysomal/total mRNA ratios after DDX6 silencing stratified by GC content.

claim: mRNAs with the most upregulated translation rate after DDX6 silencing are the least stabilized.
source: As a result, mRNAs with the most upregulated translation rate were the least stabilized, and conversely (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Correlation analysis between translation rate changes and mRNA stability changes after DDX6 silencing.

claim: mRNAs clipped to DDX6 in K562 cells are GC-rich (rs = 0.41, p<0.0001).
source: In agreement, mRNAs with a high GC content were preferentially enriched in the DDX6 CLIP experiment (rs = 0.41, p<0.0001; Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Analysis of ENCODE DDX6 CLIP dataset showing enrichment of GC-rich mRNAs.

claim: mRNAs clipped to DDX6 are particularly stabilized after DDX6 knockdown in both HEK293 and K562 cells.
source: In both HEK293 and K562 cells, the mRNAs clipped to DDX6 were particularly stabilized after DDX6 knockdown, as compared to all mRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C; Supplementary file 1, sheet3)
evidence: Comparison of fold-changes in DDX6-clipped mRNAs versus all mRNAs after DDX6 silencing.

claim: DDX6-clipped mRNAs are not translationally derepressed in HEK293 cells after DDX6 silencing.
source: while they were not translationally derepressed in HEK293 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Analysis of polysomal/total ratios for DDX6-clipped mRNAs showing no significant change.

claim: DDX6-dependent decay has a marginal preference for short transcripts (rs = -0.09, p<0.0001).
source: While DDX6-dependent decay had a marginal preference for short transcripts (rs = −0.09, p<0.0001), as a combined effect of CDS and 3'UTR length (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,F)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis between mRNA length and DDX6-dependent decay.

claim: DDX6-dependent translation repression is independent of CDS length but higher on mRNAs with long 3'UTRs (rs = 0.16, p<0.0001).
source: DDX6-dependent translation repression was independent of the CDS length but higher on mRNAs with long 3'UTRs (rs = 0.16, p<0.0001; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E,G).
evidence: Analysis of translation rate changes stratified by CDS and 3'UTR length.

claim: The GC content of both CDS and 3'UTR are similarly predictive of DDX6 sensitivity for mRNA stability.
source: Interestingly, the GC content of the CDS and the 3'UTR were similarly predictive of DDX6 sensitivity, whether for mRNA stability (rs = 0.42 and 0.40 for CDS and 3'UTR, respectively, p<0.0001 for both)
evidence: Correlation analysis comparing predictive power of CDS versus 3'UTR GC content.

claim: The GC content of both CDS and 3'UTR are similarly predictive of DDX6 sensitivity for translation repression.
source: or for translation repression (rs = −0.53 and −0.52, respectively, p<0.0001 for both), while the 5'UTR was less significant (rs = 0.18 and −0.15 for stability and translation repression, respectively, p<0.0001 for both; Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: Correlation analysis comparing predictive power of different mRNA regions for translation repression.

claim: XRN1-dependent decay preferentially acts on GC-rich mRNAs in both HeLa (rs = 0.41) and HCT116 (rs = 0.49) cells.
source: In both cell lines, XRN1-dependent decay preferentially acted on mRNAs which were GC-rich (rs = 0.41 for HeLa and 0.49 for HCT116, p<0.0001 for both; Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Analysis of mRNA fold-changes after XRN1 silencing in two different cell lines.

claim: XRN1 targets are localized out of PBs (rs = -0.35, p<0.0001).
source: and localized out of PBs (rs = −0.35, p<0.0001; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), as observed for DDX6.
evidence: Correlation analysis between XRN1 sensitivity and PB enrichment.

claim: PAT1B targets are AU-rich (rs = -0.50, p<0.0001).
source: Indeed, in contrast to DDX6 and XRN1 decay targets, PAT1B targets tended to be AU-rich (rs = −0.50, p<0.0001; Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Analysis of GC content distribution of PAT1B targets from silencing experiment.

claim: PAT1B silencing does not result in increased 5' coverage of target mRNAs.
source: To gain insight into the mechanism of regulation by PAT1B, we analyzed the read coverage in the PAT1B silencing experiment (Figure 4C) and found it to be unchanged over the whole transcriptome.
evidence: Read coverage analysis along mRNA length showing no 5' bias for PAT1B targets.

claim: XRN1 silencing results in higher 5' coverage of target mRNAs.
source: In contrast, following XRN1 silencing, the 5' coverage was higher, confirming that such an analysis can reveal 5' decay (Figure 4D).
evidence: Read coverage analysis showing increased 5' reads after XRN1 silencing.

claim: PAT1B target mRNAs have higher 5' coverage than average in control cells.
source: Of note, in control cells PAT1B target mRNAs had a higher 5' coverage than average (Figure 4C)
evidence: Read coverage analysis of PAT1B targets in control conditions.

claim: XRN1 target mRNAs have lower 5' coverage than average in control cells.
source: while XRN1 targets had a lower 5' coverage than average (Figure 4D).
evidence: Read coverage analysis of XRN1 targets in control conditions.

claim: mRNA accumulation after PAT1B silencing does not result from 5' end protection.
source: These results suggest that mRNA accumulation in the absence of PAT1B does not result from their 5' end protection.
evidence: Inference based on read coverage analysis showing no 5' bias.

claim: DDX6 is a cofactor of XRN1 5'-3' exonuclease.
source: The results suggest that DDX6 is a cofactor of XRN1 5'−3' exonuclease, whereas PAT1B affects 3' to 5' degradation.
evidence: Inference based on the similar GC-rich target preferences and read coverage patterns of DDX6 and XRN1.

claim: PAT1B affects 3' to 5' mRNA degradation.
source: The results suggest that DDX6 is a cofactor of XRN1 5'−3' exonuclease, whereas PAT1B affects 3' to 5' degradation.
evidence: Inference based on read coverage analysis and distinct target preferences compared to DDX6/XRN1.

claim: SMG6 targets are GC-rich mRNAs.
source: On the mRNA decay side (group I lists), we considered the Nonsense Mediated Decay (NMD) pathway, taking as targets the mRNAs cleaved by SMG6 (Schmidt et al., 2015)
evidence: Analysis of published SMG6 PARE data showing GC-rich targets (Figure 5A).

claim: YTHDF2 targets are GC-rich mRNAs.
source: and the m6A-associated decay pathways, using the targets of the YTHDF2 reader defined by CLIP (Wang et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: Analysis of published YTHDF2 CLIP data showing GC-rich targets (Figure 5A).

claim: mRNAs with 5'UTR-located G4 motifs are preferential substrates of XRN1.
source: We also analyzed mRNAs with a 5'UTR-located G4 motif, which have been shown to be preferential substrates of murine XRN1 in vitro (Bashkirov et al., 1997).
evidence: Citation to previous work showing G4-containing mRNAs are XRN1 substrates.

claim: TOP mRNAs are GC-rich.
source: On the translation regulation side (group II lists), we analyzed the TOP mRNAs, whose translation is controlled by a TOP motif at the 5' extremity (Thoreen et al., 2012)
evidence: Analysis showing TOP mRNAs have high GC content (Figure 5A).

claim: Group I list mRNAs (SMG6, YTHDF2, G4) are GC-rich compared to all mRNAs.
source: Intriguingly, compared to all mRNAs, group I list mRNAs were GC-rich, as well as TOP mRNAs and ATXN2 targets, whereas all other group II lists were AU-rich (Figure 5A).
evidence: Comparative analysis of GC content distributions across different target lists.

claim: Most group II list mRNAs (except TOP, ATXN2, 4E-T) are AU-rich.
source: Intriguingly, compared to all mRNAs, group I list mRNAs were GC-rich, as well as TOP mRNAs and ATXN2 targets, whereas all other group II lists were AU-rich (Figure 5A).
evidence: Comparative analysis of GC content distributions showing AU-rich bias for most translation regulator targets.

claim: Group I list mRNAs are dependent on DDX6 and XRN1 but not PAT1B for stability.
source: Group I list mRNAs tended to be dependent on DDX6 and XRN1 but not on PAT1B for stability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D)
evidence: Analysis of fold-changes after DDX6, XRN1, and PAT1B silencing for group I targets.

claim: Group I list mRNAs do not accumulate in PBs.
source: They did not accumulate in PBs and their translation rate was independent of DDX6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment and translation rate changes for group I targets.

claim: Group II list mRNAs (except TOP, ATXN2, 4E-T) are stabilized following PAT1B silencing.
source: Group II list mRNAs, except TOP mRNAs, ATXN2 and 4E-T targets, had the exact mirror fate compared to group I lists: they were stabilized following PAT1B silencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Analysis of fold-changes after PAT1B silencing for group II targets.

claim: Group II list mRNAs (except TOP, ATXN2, 4E-T) are enriched in PBs.
source: they were enriched in PBs and translationally more active after DDX6 silencing (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment and translation rate changes for group II targets.

claim: ATXN2 targets are excluded from PBs.
source: ATXN2 is a major DDX6 partner, but one which is excluded from PBs (Ayache et al., 2015; Nonhoff et al., 2007), consistent with its targets also being excluded from PBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment for ATXN2 targets combined with citation to previous work on ATXN2 localization.

claim: 4E-T targets are markedly enriched in PBs.
source: Its targets were markedly enriched in PBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), though, intriguingly, poorly affected by PAT1B silencing in terms of stability (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), or by DDX6 silencing in terms of translation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Analysis showing high PB enrichment but low sensitivity to DDX6/PAT1B for 4E-T targets.

claim: PB localization is not sufficient for mRNA to have PAT1B-dependent stability and DDX6-dependent translation repression.
source: This dissociation between PB localization and mRNA fate indicated that PB recruitment is not sufficient for an mRNA to have a PAT1B-dependent stability and DDX6-dependent translation repression.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that 4E-T targets are in PBs but not regulated by PAT1B/DDX6.

claim: In HEK293 cells, suboptimal codons do not enhance DDX6 recruitment to trigger mRNA decay.
source: Thus, in HEK293 cells, this mechanism seemed to account for a minor part of DDX6-dependent decay, if any, as also found in mouse stem cells (Freimer et al., 2018).
evidence: Analysis showing weak correlation between polysomal retention and DDX6-dependent decay, combined with citation to supporting work.

claim: AGO protein targets are AU-rich.
source: The mRNA targets of AGO proteins were AU-rich, as observed for most group II RBPs, and this was also true for the targets of most miRNAs when analyzed separately (Figure 5C).
evidence: Analysis of GC content distribution for AGO and miRNA targets.

claim: AGO targets tend to accumulate in PBs.
source: The AGO targets tended to accumulate in PBs (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C; note that the number of AGO4 targets was too small to reach statistical significance)
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment for AGO1-4 targets.

claim: AGO target translation rate is DDX6-dependent.
source: and their translation rate was DDX6-dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Analysis of translation rate changes after DDX6 silencing for AGO targets.

claim: Only AGO2 targets are marginally DDX6-dependent for stability.
source: In terms of stability, only AGO2 targets were marginally DDX6-dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: Analysis of mRNA stability changes after DDX6 silencing for different AGO targets.

claim: AGO target stability is PAT1B-dependent.
source: In contrast, their stability was PAT1B-dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: Analysis of mRNA stability changes after PAT1B silencing for AGO targets.

claim: miRNA targets generally accumulate in PBs, have DDX6-dependent translation, and PAT1B-dependent stability.
source: The targets of the 22 miRNAs had a behavior overall similar to the targets of AGO proteins, with accumulation in PBs, DDX6-dependent translation, and PAT1B rather than DDX6- or XRN1-dependent stability (Figure 5D).
evidence: Comprehensive analysis of miRNA targets across multiple datasets.

claim: Different miRNAs show variation in the extent of PB storage of their targets.
source: However, our analysis revealed some differences between miRNAs, particularly in terms of extent of PB storage (Figure 5—figure supplement 3H)
evidence: Comparative analysis of PB enrichment across different miRNA target sets.

claim: miR21-5p targets are particularly AU-rich and strongly enriched in PBs.
source: at the two extremes, miR21-5p targets were particularly AU-rich and strongly enriched in PBs
evidence: Analysis of GC content and PB enrichment for miR21-5p targets.

claim: miR-99b-5p targets are the most GC-rich among analyzed miRNA targets and not enriched in PBs.
source: while the targets of miR-99b-5p, the most GC-rich in these sets, were not.
evidence: Analysis of GC content and PB enrichment for miR-99b-5p targets.

claim: The median GC content of miRNA targets correlates with the GC content of the miRNA itself.
source: Interestingly, we noted that the median GC content of the miRNA targets correlated with the GC content of the miRNA itself (Figure 5—figure supplement 5F).
evidence: Correlation analysis between miRNA sequence GC content and target GC content.

claim: mRNA GC content is a major parameter for PB localization and regulation by DDX6, XRN1 and PAT1B in steady-state conditions.
source: Altogether, our analysis showed that, in steady-state conditions, mRNA GC content is a major parameter in terms of PB localization and regulation by DDX6, XRN1 and PAT1B, while the presence of binding sites for regulatory proteins makes subsidiary contributions.
evidence: Summary inference based on the observation that targets of specific RBPs generally behave according to their GC content.

claim: The fold changes of RBP targets generally fall close to the tendency plot based on GC content only.
source: Surprisingly, the fold changes of the targets of particular RBPs generally fell very close to the tendency plot based on GC content only.
evidence: Analysis comparing behavior of specific RBP targets to GC-content-binned transcriptome (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).

claim: AU-rich mRNAs excluded from PBs are more sensitive to XRN1-dependent decay than other AU-rich transcripts.
source: Compared to other similarly AU-rich transcripts, these mRNAs were indeed more sensitive to XRN1-dependent decay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Analysis of XRN1 sensitivity for AU-rich mRNAs stratified by PB localization.

claim: AU-rich mRNAs excluded from PBs are not more sensitive to DDX6-dependent decay.
source: However they were not more sensitive to DDX6-dependent decay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Analysis of DDX6 sensitivity for AU-rich mRNAs stratified by PB localization.

claim: XRN1 preference for GC-rich mRNAs is at least partly related to their exclusion from PBs.
source: This suggested that XRN1 preference for GC-rich mRNAs is at least in part related to their exclusion from PBs
evidence: Inference based on observation that PB-excluded AU-rich mRNAs are more XRN1-sensitive.

claim: DDX6 has a true preference for GC-rich mRNAs independent of PB localization.
source: whereas DDX6 has a true preference for GC-rich mRNAs.
evidence: Inference based on observation that PB-excluded AU-rich mRNAs are not more DDX6-sensitive.

claim: PB-excluded AU-rich mRNAs are strongly enriched for genes encoding secreted proteins and proteins associated with membranous organelles.
source: Interestingly, these PB-excluded AU-rich mRNAs were strongly enriched in mRNAs encoding secreted proteins and proteins associated with membranous organelles, with GO categories related to mitochondria, intracellular organelles and extracellular matrix proteins representing up to 36% of the transcripts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Gene ontology analysis of PB-excluded AU-rich mRNAs.

claim: The correlation between lncRNA GC content and PB accumulation (rs = -0.20) is much weaker than for mRNAs (rs = -0.64).
source: The correlation between their GC content and PB accumulation was significant (rs = −0.20, p<0.0001), but much weaker than that observed for mRNAs (−0.64, Figure 1B) or 3'UTRs (−0.55, Figure 1D) (−0.20 and −0.55 are significantly different, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation coefficients between lncRNAs and mRNAs.

claim: AU-rich lncRNAs poorly accumulate in PBs.
source: In fact, AU-rich lncRNAs poorly accumulated in PBs, while GC-rich lncRNAs were excluded (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment for lncRNAs stratified by GC content.

claim: The coding capacity of mRNAs is important for PB localization.
source: This suggested that the coding capacity of mRNAs was important for PB localization.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that lncRNAs show weaker GC-dependent PB accumulation than mRNAs.

claim: The CDS GC content is systematically lower in PB mRNAs than PB-excluded mRNAs across all 3'UTR GC content groups.
source: Their GC3 was systematically much lower in PB mRNAs than in PB-excluded mRNAs, with differences ranging between 9% and 13% GC (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Analysis of CDS GC3 stratified by 3'UTR GC content and PB localization.

claim: The importance of 3'UTR GC content for PB localization becomes visible only for CDS with GC3 higher than 50%.
source: The importance of the 3'UTR GC content became visible only for GC3 higher than 50% GC (note that GC3 median value is 59% GC), with AU-rich 3'UTR allowing for their accumulation in PBs despite a GC-rich CDS (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Analysis of 3'UTR GC content stratified by CDS GC3 and PB localization.

claim: Haplo-insufficient mRNAs are significantly enriched in PBs.
source: Using these scores, we found that haplo-insufficient mRNAs were indeed significantly enriched in PBs (Figure 6C).
evidence: Analysis of PB enrichment using published haplo-insufficiency scores.

claim: AU-rich Rluc reporter mRNA has 4.5-fold lower protein yield than GC-rich version despite similar mRNA levels.
source: In agreement with our previous analyses, Rluc protein yield was considerably reduced (4.5-fold) using the AU-rich rather than the GC-rich version of the CDS, despite similar mRNA levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: Experimental measurement of luciferase activity and mRNA levels for reporter constructs.

claim: PBs containing AU-rich Rluc mRNA clusters are five times more frequent than those containing GC-rich Rluc mRNA.
source: PBs containing clusters of Rluc mRNA molecules were five times more frequent using the AU-rich than the GC-rich version of the CDS (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: Quantification of PBs containing reporter mRNAs by smiFISH in multiple experiments.

claim: AU-rich RNA increases the number of PB-like granules in cell-free extract in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The AU-rich RNA increased the number of PB-like granules in a dose-dependent manner, while GC-rich RNA prevented their formation.
evidence: Flow cytometry quantification of PB-like granules formed in vitro with different RNA types.

claim: GC-rich RNA prevents the formation of PB-like granules in cell-free extract.
source: The AU-rich RNA increased the number of PB-like granules in a dose-dependent manner, while GC-rich RNA prevented their formation.
evidence: Flow cytometry quantification showing decreased granule formation with GC-rich RNA.

claim: Uncapped non-polyadenylated AU-rich RNA specifically favors condensation of DDX6-dependent granules containing LSM14A.
source: Therefore, in the complex lysate environment and at 0°C, uncapped non-polyadenylated AU-rich RNA specifically favor the condensation of granules that are DDX6-dependent and contain LSM14A, two proteins that play a major role in the assembly of cellular PBs.
evidence: Summary of in vitro reconstitution experiments showing AU-rich RNA promotes PB-like granule formation.

claim: Low GC content in the CDS acts through codon usage and low translation efficiency for PB localization.
source: Low GC content in the CDS likely acts, at least in part, through codon usage and low translation efficiency.
evidence: Inference based on correlations between GC content, codon usage, and protein yield.

claim: Low GC content in the 3'UTR could allow for binding of RBPs with affinity for AU-rich motifs and/or influence RNA secondary structure.
source: In the 3'UTR low GC content could allow for the binding of RBPs with affinity for AU-rich motifs and/or influence RNA secondary structure.
evidence: Speculation about mechanisms by which 3'UTR GC content affects PB localization.

claim: GC-rich mRNAs are excluded from PBs and controlled at the mRNA level by DDX6 and XRN1.
source: As schematized in Figure 7, GC-rich mRNAs are excluded from PBs and mostly controlled at the mRNA level by a mechanism involving the helicase DDX6 and the 5'−3' exonuclease XRN1.
evidence: Summary of multiple analyses showing coordinated behavior of GC-rich mRNAs.

claim: AU-rich mRNAs are enriched in PBs and controlled at the translation level by DDX6.
source: In contrast, AU-rich mRNAs are enriched in PBs and rather controlled at the level of translation by a mechanism also involving DDX6
evidence: Summary of multiple analyses showing coordinated behavior of AU-rich mRNAs.

claim: AU-rich mRNA stability depends on PAT1B and likely 3' decay.
source: while their accumulation tend to depend on a mechanism involving the DDX6 partner PAT1B and most likely 3' decay.
evidence: Summary inference based on PAT1B silencing data and read coverage analysis.

claim: NMD and m6A-associated mRNA decay pathways tend to target GC-rich mRNAs.
source: Accordingly, NMD and m6A-associated mRNA decay pathways tend to target GC-rich mRNAs
evidence: Analysis of SMG6 and YTHDF2 targets showing GC-rich bias.

claim: Most sequence-specific translation regulators and miRNAs tend to target AU-rich mRNAs.
source: while most sequence-specific translation regulators and miRNAs tend to target AU-rich mRNAs.
evidence: Analysis of multiple RBP and miRNA target sets showing AU-rich bias.

claim: 5' mRNA decay preferentially controls mRNAs with optimal translation, which are mostly GC-rich.
source: Thus, 5' mRNA decay appears to control preferentially mRNAs with optimal translation, which are mostly GC-rich
evidence: Summary inference based on correlations between GC content, codon usage, and decay pathways.

claim: Translation regulation is mostly used to control mRNAs with limiting translational efficiency, which are AU-rich.
source: whereas translation regulation is mostly used to control mRNAs with limiting translational efficiency, which are AU-rich.
evidence: Summary inference based on correlations between GC content, codon usage, and translation regulation.

claim: The model of GC-content-dependent post-transcriptional regulation only applies to pathways involving PBs, XRN1, DDX6 and PAT1B.
source: It should be stressed that this model only applies to post-transcriptional regulation pathways that involve PBs, XRN1, DDX6 and PAT1B.
evidence: Explicit limitation of the scope of the proposed model.

claim: The model was consistent in proliferating cells of various origins.
source: Moreover, while the analysis was consistent in proliferating cells of various origins, giving rise to a general model
evidence: Observation that similar patterns were seen in HEK293, HeLa, HCT116, and K562 cells.

claim: Changes in cell physiology may rely on different post-transcriptional regulation mechanisms than the described model.
source: it is possible that changes in cell physiology, for instance at particular developmental stages or during differentiation, rely on a different mechanism.
evidence: Speculation about limitations of the model under different cellular conditions.

claim: The high number of low usage codons in PB mRNAs is a likely determinant of their low protein yield.
source: Furthermore, the high number of low usage codons in PB mRNAs is a likely determinant of their low protein yield.
evidence: Inference based on correlation between low usage codon number and protein yield.

claim: Suboptimal translation of AU-rich CDS makes mRNAs optimal targets for translation regulation.
source: We speculate that suboptimal translation of AU-rich CDS makes mRNAs optimal targets for translation regulation, since any control mechanism has to rely on a limiting step.
evidence: Speculation about why AU-rich mRNAs are preferentially regulated at translation level.

claim: Optimally translated transcripts would be better controlled at the level of stability.
source: Conversely, optimally translated transcripts would be better controlled at the level of stability.
evidence: Speculation about why GC-rich mRNAs are preferentially regulated at stability level.

claim: DDX6 unwinding of GC-rich double-stranded regions facilitates XRN1 progression.
source: It is tempting to propose rather that, by unwinding GC-rich double-stranded regions over the entire length of the mRNA, DDX6 facilitates XRN1 progression.
evidence: Speculation about the molecular mechanism of DDX6 function in decay.

claim: UPF1 helicase preferentially affects decay of GC-rich mRNAs.
source: UPF1, another RNA helicase involved in mRNA decay, has also been shown to preferentially affect the decay of GC-rich mRNAs (Imamachi et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous work showing similar GC-rich preference for another helicase.

claim: NMD pathway targets show GC-rich bias restricted to 3'UTR regions.
source: The same observation was made for targets of the NMD pathway, which involves UPF1, SMG6 and SMG7 (Colombo et al., 2017). Although the bias in these cases was restricted to the 3'UTR regions
evidence: Citation to previous work on NMD targets.

claim: DDX6 could act in concert with other helicases for decay of GC-rich mRNAs.
source: it suggests that DDX6 could act in concert with other helicases for decay of GC-rich mRNAs.
evidence: Speculation based on observations of multiple helicases affecting GC-rich mRNA decay.

claim: Skin fibroblasts from patients with DDX6 missense mutations show significant accumulation of GC-rich mRNAs.
source: Noteworthily, in agreement with the present study in cell lines, skin fibroblasts from patients with DDX6 missense mutations also showed significant accumulation of GC-rich mRNAs (Balak et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to clinical study showing similar GC-dependent effects in patient cells.

claim: Yeast XRN1 associates with ribosomes and decays mRNAs during translation.
source: Of particular relevance, a recent study showed that yeast XRN1 associates with ribosomes and decays mRNAs during translation (Tesina et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to recent work on yeast XRN1 mechanism.

claim: If the ribosome-associated decay mechanism is conserved in human, it would explain why XRN1 preferentially acts on GC-rich mRNAs.
source: If the mechanism is conserved in human, it would explain why XRN1 preferentially acts on GC-rich mRNAs, since they are the most actively translated mRNAs.
evidence: Speculation about implications of yeast findings for human cells.

claim: Dhh1/DDX6 and Pat1/PAT1B decay targets poorly overlap in yeast.
source: A recent yeast study also showed that Dhh1/DDX6 and Pat1/PAT1B decay targets poorly overlap, suggesting the existence of two separate pathways in yeast as well (He et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to yeast study showing similar separation of decay pathways.

claim: Both Pat1 and Dhh1 targets were poorly translated in yeast, while only PAT1B targets were poorly translated in human cells.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms may differ in the two organisms, since both Pat1 and Dhh1 targets were poorly translated in yeast, while only PAT1B targets were poorly translated in our study.
evidence: Comparison of current findings with published yeast data.

claim: Tethered PAT1B decreases reporter mRNA abundance through enhanced deadenylation and decapping in human cells.
source: Previous studies reported that tethered PAT1B decreases the abundance of a reporter mRNA in human cells, as a result of enhanced deadenylation and decapping (Ozgur et al., 2010; Kamenska et al., 2014; Totaro et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to previous tethering experiments.

claim: Genome-wide evidence in yeast suggests transcripts up-regulated in cells lacking Pat1 or Lsm1 are efficiently decayed from 3' to 5' rather than by Xrn1.
source: Interestingly, genome-wide evidence in yeast too suggests that following decapping a significant fraction of the transcripts up-regulated in cells lacking Pat1 or Lsm1 is efficiently decayed from 3' to 5', rather than by the 5'−3' Xrn1 exonuclease (He et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to yeast genome-wide study supporting 3' to 5' decay mechanism.

claim: CLIP experiments in yeast show preference for Pat1 and Lsm1 binding to the 3' end of mRNAs.
source: Moreover, CLIP experiments in yeast showed a preference for Pat1 and Lsm1 binding to the 3' end of mRNAs (Mitchell et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to yeast CLIP data showing 3' end binding preference.

claim: PAT1B affects mRNA stability in human cells prominently through 3' to 5' decay.
source: Altogether, we therefore favor the possibility that the mechanism by which PAT1B affects mRNA stability in human cells relies prominently on 3' to 5' decay.
evidence: Inference based on read coverage analysis and comparison with yeast data.

claim: PAT1B-mediated decay could involve the CCR4/CNOT deadenylase and LSM1-7 complexes.
source: It could involve the CCR4/CNOT deadenylase and the LMS1-7 complexes, as, despite their low abundance or small size, CNOT1 and LSM2/4 had high scores in our previous PAT1B interactome analysis (Vindry et al., 2017; Vindry et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculation based on previous interactome data.

claim: ARE-BPs could behave as enhancers or inhibitors of PAT1B activity in mRNA decay.
source: Altogether, these observations raise the possibility that ARE-BPs behave either as enhancers or inhibitors of PAT1B activity in mRNA decay.
evidence: Speculation about the relationship between ARE-BPs and PAT1B.

claim: The miRNA pathway could activate PAT1B activity.
source: Similarly, the miRNA pathway could activate this PAT1B activity.
evidence: Speculation about miRNA pathway interaction with PAT1B.

claim: DDX6 contributes to repression of maternal mRNAs in Xenopus oocytes as a component of the CPEB complex.
source: In Xenopus oocytes, DDX6 contributes to the repression of maternal mRNAs, as a component of the well characterized CPEB complex (Minshall et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation to previous work on DDX6 function in Xenopus.

claim: Me31B/DDX6 represses translation of thousands of mRNAs during early maternal to zygotic transition in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, Me31B/DDX6 represses the translation of thousands of mRNAs during the early stages of the maternal to zygotic transition (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous work on DDX6 function in Drosophila.

claim: DDX6 collaborates with FMRP and AGO proteins for translation repression in fly neurons.
source: It also collaborates with FMRP and AGO proteins for translation repression in fly neurons (Barbee et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to previous work on DDX6 in neuronal translation regulation.

claim: DDX6 is a general co-factor of the miRNA pathway in mammals.
source: In mammals, DDX6 is a general co-factor of the miRNA pathway (Chen et al., 2014; Mathys et al., 2014; Kamenska et al., 2016; Chu and Rana, 2006).
evidence: Citation to multiple studies establishing DDX6 role in miRNA pathway.

claim: 4E-T function in PBs is partly independent of DDX6.
source: First, this suggests that 4E-T function in PBs is partly independent of DDX6, agreeing with the previous observation that some PBs can still form when the DDX6 interaction domain of 4E-T is mutated (Kamenska et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference based on current data combined with citation to previous mutational study.

claim: PB localization and translation repression by DDX6 can be separated to some extent.
source: Second, it indicates that PB localization and translation repression by DDX6 can be separated, at least to some extent.
evidence: Inference based on observation that 4E-T targets are in PBs but not DDX6-regulated.

claim: Long CDS could favor mRNA recruitment in PBs by decreasing translation efficiency.
source: Long CDS could favor mRNA recruitment in PBs by decreasing translation efficiency, and hence increasing the fraction of polysome-free mRNAs.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism linking CDS length to PB recruitment.

claim: Long 3'UTR should increase the probability of binding translation regulators, contributing to PB recruitment.
source: Long 3'UTR should increase the probability of binding translation regulators, contributing also to PB recruitment.
evidence: Speculation about mechanism linking 3'UTR length to PB recruitment.

claim: DDX6 and LSM14A coat repressed mRNAs at multiple positions according to their length.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that we and others have previously proposed from biochemical experiments and electron microscopy imaging that DDX6 and its partner LSM14A coat repressed mRNAs at multiple positions, according to their length (Ernoult-Lange et al., 2012; Götze et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to previous biochemical and imaging studies.

claim: The GC-rich part of the human genome only emerged in amniotes.
source: While PBs have been observed in very diverse eukaryotes, animal and vegetal, the GC-rich part of the human genome only emerged in amniotes (the ancestor of birds and mammals) (Duret et al., 2002).
evidence: Citation to previous work on genome evolution.

claim: In yeast, C. elegans, Drosophila and Xenopus, genes have a narrow GC content distribution, most often AU-rich.
source: In more distant organisms, such as yeast, C. elegans, Drosophila or Xenopus, genes have a narrow GC content distribution, most often AU-rich (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Analysis of GC content distributions across multiple organisms.

claim: Distinct modes of mRNA stability control depending on GC content may have evolved more recently than the conservation of DDX6, XRN1 and PAT1B proteins.
source: Thus, despite the conservation of the DDX6, XRN1 and to a lesser extent PAT1B proteins in eukaryotes, distinct modes of mRNA stability control depending on GC content may have evolved more recently.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary analysis of genome GC content and protein conservation.

claim: The enzymatic properties of DDX6 could have adapted to the higher GC content of human transcripts.
source: Moreover, the enzymatic properties of DDX6 could have adapted to the higher GC content of human transcripts.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary adaptation of DDX6.

claim: The GC-rich part of the human genome was acquired through GC-biased gene conversion linked with meiotic recombination.
source: The GC-rich part of the human genome was acquired through GC-biased gene conversion (gBGC), a non-selective process linked with meiotic recombination affecting GC content evolution (Duret and Galtier, 2009).
evidence: Citation to previous work on gBGC mechanism.

claim: mRNA base composition and PB enrichment are associated independently of meiotic recombination or genomic context.
source: However, our analysis showed that mRNA base composition and PB enrichment are associated independently of meiotic recombination or the genomic context.
evidence: Statistical analysis controlling for meiotic recombination and genomic context.

claim: The genome of higher eukaryotes has evolved partly to facilitate control of regulators at the translation level by limiting their protein yield.
source: We therefore put forward a model where the genome of higher eukaryotes has evolved partly to facilitate the control of regulators at the translation level, by limiting their protein yield.
evidence: Speculation about evolutionary implications of GC content effects on translation.

claim: In human, GC content shapes mRNA fate and its control in a strikingly coherent system.
source: Regardless, the overall outcome of our study is that in human the GC content, a feature written in the genome, shapes in part mRNA fate and its control in a strikingly coherent system.
evidence: Summary statement integrating all findings about GC content effects.
